Larry Page is a former founder and executive of Google, a web search engine. Google provides both a web search engine and a range of computational and processing platforms, including natural language processing, data mining, and search algorithms for web and mobile devices. As a co-founder of Google, Larry Page had primarily focused on developing the search engine's core algorithms. In 2014, Larry Page co-founded X, which was acquired by Alphabet (formerly Google). X, a subsidiary of Alphabet maintained and developed the search algorithms, including a variety of web and software development. However, X's research focus and its set of proper offerings also included a number of other areas, such as renewable energy, hardware design, and the field of neuro stem cells. The projects of Larry Page and Alphabet (formerly Google) in these areas were typically related to Larry Page's vision, and he has been publicly discussing and expressing his ideas in various articles and interviews.

Based on the Cooking for Geeks article about the science of caramel:

Caramel is just sugar that's been slowly cooked, which turns it a golden brown and gives it a sweet, buttery flavor. The high temperatures of the cooking process make all the water in the sugar evaporate, which leaves the molecules in the syrup free to react and form all sorts of chemical bonds. When you cook sugar, different molecules with different colors and flavors are created, in a process called browning. Browning is actually a combination of two reactions: polymerization and Maillard reactions.

Polymerization happens when sugar molecules link together to create large sugar chains. As the sugar chains get bigger, they become too heavy to stay liquid, so they turn into that crystalline stuff you don't want in your caramel. So, to keep your sugar from crystallizing, you need to add some water, which will keep the sugar molecules from getting too big. This is called a sugar syrup.

Maillard reactions, on the other hand, are what produce the rich, golden brown color in caramel, as well as the flavor. They happen between sugars and amino groups (amino groups are a part of proteins, and caramelizing sugar and protein is the goal in caramelizing cream). As with polymerization, high temperatures speed up the Maillard reactions, so if you want a deep caramel color, don't skimp on the cooking time.

To make a caramel sauce, you'll need:

- 2/3 to 2 1/3 cups (135 to 450 g) granulated sugar
- 1/4 to 1/2 cup (30 to 60 ml) water
- 1/4 cup (57 g) butter, cut into pieces
- 1/4 cup (50 to 60 g) white granulated sugar

Follow these simple steps:

1. Preheat your oven: To a 125 to 150° C (260 to 300° F) degree bake. It's best to check your oven's temperature variability before cooking.

2. Get baking: Line a baking dish with foil and bake the sugar syrup in the oven, stirring (with a heatproof spatula that can handle the high temperature) frequently with a rubber spatula, until the syrup looks like honey and the Maillard reactions are to your liking. The exact cooking time will depend on your oven, but the sugar will reach its "honey color" stage between 30 and 40 minutes.

3. Make the topping: While your caramel is still warm, stir in the butter and cream until you have a smooth, blended sauce. Do this over ice water, stirring constantly, the sauce should become thick and shiny. Make sure the caramel is still warm, not hot. If it's too hot, the sauce may be too loose. If it's too cool, the sauce may have a grainy texture.

Caramel sauce will keep for a long time in the refrigerator, but it will crystallize, so you'll need to reheat it over low heat in the microwave or in a saucepan, stirring constantly, until it's in a smooth, pourable state. If you have leftover caramel sauce, you can store it in the refrigerator for up to 2 months.

Caramel sauce recipe taken from "Cook's Illustrated" (the magazine version of "Cook's Bible") and this is the recipe for a while now, so it's trusted. But this past December, a home cook taught me a new method, which I had to share with you, as it's kind of an "a-ha!". She brought brownie sauce, and when I asked her how she made it, she said, "I just added a little bit of cream to the basic Cook's Illustrated caramel sauce." That's the recipe she used for some time, but then she experimented and found that the longer you heat the cream, the grainier the caramel sauce will be. So now she heats cream and sugar separately, and the result is fantastic. I've made it a dozen times, and it's always gotten rave reviews.

1. Get your pan ready: Wear an oven mitt, and place a heatproof 1/3-cup (80-ml) baking dish in the upper third of a conventional oven, and turn the oven on to 300°F (150 °C). Leave the oven mitt on your hand, so you don't burn yourself when you take the hot baking dish out with it.

2. Make the water: Set a 1-cup (240 ml) liquid cup next to the oven. You'll need it in a moment.

3. Get started: Once the oven and baking dish are in the oven, reduce the heat to 275 °F (135 °C). The oven dish should now be warm (but not too hot) to the touch, and ready for you to pour in the ingredients.

4. Add the sugar: Pour 2/3 cup (150 g) of granulated sugar into a small (4-5 inch/ 10-12 cm) heatproof glass measuring cup. The cup should be just large enough to fit into your baking dish, so the sugar is poured into the baking dish. I use a small, 1-cup (240 ml) glass liquid measuring cup.

5. Make the syrup: Place the measuring cup in the oven, on the baking dish. Stir the sugar with a heatproof rubber spatula until the sugar has completely dissolved and the syrup looks clear, about 5 minutes. (If you have a convection oven, turn your oven down to 250 °F (125 °C), and use the bake setting. You don't need to stir as frequently, so the syrup will take about 10 minutes to reach a clear syrup stage.)

6. Add the butter: Turn off the oven, and stir the butter into the syrup until it is completely melted and incorporated into the syrup. Watch as the butter melts. When the butter is almost melted, and the sugar dissolved, remove the cup from the oven. If you have a convection, turn off the oven (if you still feel heat, let the oven and the butter rest for 1 minute) and continue as above. If you get any sugar on the bottom of the cup, don't worry. It's just crystalline sugar, and won't affect the recipe. Just be careful not to get any on the inside of the measuring cup.

7. Add the cream: Remove the cup from the rubber spatula, and place the cup on a heatproof surface. Stir in the cream until it is completely blended and the caramel sauce is smooth.

8. Done: Carefully take the caramel sauce out of the cup, and pour it into a jar. Your caramel sauce will keep for 2 months in the refrigerator. Just before you're ready to use the sauce, give it a stir

In 1895, H.G. Wells published "The Time Machine," a story about a "time traveler" who journeys over 800,000 years into the future, to an Earth in the distant past, a dead and dying world. The time traveler, the story's narrator, witnesses the Earth's end, and the extinction of the human race, as he journeys through time, from the familiar world of 1895, to a remote, dying world, 804,000 years in the future. In "The Time Machine," Wells poses a fundamental question, "Is humanity's future secure?" He does not believe so, and paints a vivid word picture of a dying world, and a dead humanity, the end of civilization.

Wells's "The Time Machine" is a work of fiction, but it is also a work of political science. The narrator, the time traveler, travels from Victorian England to a distant, dying Earth, 800,000 years after humanity's end. The future humanity is divided into two species: the White (Caucasian) race, which has degenerated, both mentally and physically, and the Eloi, a peaceful, childlike, and beautiful, yet feeble-minded race. Why he is a communist (he is a communist, he was a member of a government, he was a high-ranking functionary of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia, and so on), I could understand, but I don't agree with him, especially, on his stand that the man made the greatest advances in the field of science and technology for the first time in the Middle Ages, and that there is no hope for more advancements in any field of the others, except skepticism, in the 1960s. I may partially agree that the future will be different, and that it is useless to make any far-reaching statements, for, as above, uncertainty is inherent in human life, and both the present and the just arrived past always, at all times, and under normal circumstances, are shrouded in uncertainty. But my father's philosophical and religious views, as he openly expressed them, struck me in a very negative way. Once, when I was about 15, I had the opportunity to discuss, by correspondence, with a distinguished English mathematician, John V. Neale, and I asked him "When will the year end, and what do you think about the state of science and the future of mankind?" and he wrote in his answer, that, due to high birth-rate, and some other circumstances, the end of the century was not promising, and that there was not much hope for the future, because the world was coming to an end. I expected some kind of a yes, but I was not so disappointed, when I read the second sentence, which said: "You are, no doubt, already aware of the approach of the Millennium." I was not aware of that, but I replied, that the millennium has nothing to do with the end of the century, that a new century comes every 100 years, and a millennium, never. He was surprised, and after some more exchange of letters, he never answered to my mathematical questions, and I to his, and that was the end of that.

So, I was sorry that I had not read a more extensive treatise on mathematics by John Neale, in order for me to understand, what he thought about the coming of the millennium. But, as I was young, I knew, and I knew, at that, that I would not read, but write, in my own, in order to express my views. I started to write, when I was 14, and I chose my father's profession as something I would never want to be, but as something very useful, for which a few people with talent were needed, and the country would always need them. I also knew, that I would never be one of them.

So, I opened my new journal, and I wrote, in my first sentence, "I shall not write about politics." That, indeed, was a common way among the engaged people at the time, as even a person not shunned from taking part in political life, and usually, even the active revolutionaries and terrorists, and Nihilists. At the time, the 1990s, that was a kind of a "generally accepted truth" (as Russians say), and I, too, would have said that, and probably add, "I shall write about my life, about love, about the world, about everything, except politics." I could, but I am wrong at this, and this time I will say, I regret, when I first read this, 25 years later. I should have said, "I shall write about the world, about everything, except what the authorities, in their "generally accepted truth," say must not be written about."

But, I did not regret that, a quarter of a century later, when I reread what I wrote 25 years ago. I even thought that, if I still had that first journal, I would keep it, because there was a lot of interesting and valuable in it. It was a 140-page A5-size notebook, with yellow paper and a red cover, and on the first page, in the middle of that first page, was the word I wrote: "not."

When I read, now, that first "not," I thought, "I wonder, did I write here, perhaps, something like 'I shall not write,' or even, 'I shall not write about...'? No, I did not. "Not" - and no more.

Why did I need that "not" at the beginning? I am not sure, and for the sake of this, let me look if there are other words at my disposal: "peremptorily," "absolutely," "definitely," "categorically," "under no circumstances," "in no way," Houblon, also known as hops, is a component added in the wort, whether as a primary (usually) or secondary (less often) addition to beer. The term hops throughout the hops addition is a statement about the chemical nature of the plant, specifically a flavon (called a hop flavanol) that comprises the alylphenyl group of the free molecule. The hop variety widely varies from one another in their composition, with the primary difference in aged hops being the level of one or more (mainly phenolic primary, primary and secondary, hops in English) constituents (phenolic) at the end of aging (age) in beer.

In 1985, I was a first-year graduate student, and I spent the summer as I usually did, teaching at Cornell College, then a liberal arts college in Iowa, where I held a part-time position. One of my duties was to teach a small recitation section for two first-year students, one of whom (from that time on) was interested in mathematics. This was the beginning of my career, and that particular experience was not particularly remarkable, except that one of the two students I was teaching was a young woman who, as far as I remember, had few interests outside of class but a heart full of affection within it, and who, in class, was deeply interested and eager to learn. At the time, I was teaching calculus, a course this student was taking, and I remember that, during the first lecture, she asked, "When will we need this?" I replied, "You will need this if you wish to continue on in mathematics." She then asked, "Why?" I thought for a moment, and then replied, "Well, for one thing, mathematics is all around us, hidden in the most surprising places." She then asked, "Such as?" and I spent the next ten minutes or so giving her example after example. I recall mentioning the following: in which of the following should you be concerned about mathematics:

1. If a friend invites you to play a round of golf, and you want to keep track of the score.

2. If you want to find the distance of a canyon, the height of a mountain, or the width of a valley.

3. If you want to find the amount of interest on a loan.

4. If you want to find the speed of a car, or its acceleration, or its top speed.

5. If you want to build a bridge that can support ten trains, each composed of 100 boxcars, each weighing 25,000 kilograms.

6. If you want to design a radio, a television, a telephone, a cellular phone, a computer, and so on.

7. If you want to investigate why a room is too hot or too cold.

8. If you are a physician, to find a correct dosage for a patient, to measure a patient's temperature, to examine the distribution of a disease, to test blood, to test urine, and so on.

9. If you are an astronomer, to find the position of a planet, to measure the diameter of a star, to find the distance of a galaxy, and so on.

10. If you are a chemist, to measure specific quantities of substances, to test solutions, and so on.

11. If you are an engineer, to design a more efficient engine, to improve the quality of a fabric, to design better light bulbs, and so on.

12. If you are a biologist, to investigate the size of a population, to test the quality of a food supply, and so on.

13. If you are a physicist, to design better instruments, to improve the efficiency of a machine, to improve the quality of a material, and so on.

14. If you are a statistician, to analyze data, to test the quality of a material, and so on.

15. If you are a lawyer, to determine a winner in an election, to test the accuracy of a scale, and so on.

16. If you are a politician, to determine the number of people who voted, to test the strength of a bridge, and so on.

17. If you are a stockbroker, to determine the cost of building a dam, to analyze data, and so on.

18. If you are a city planner, to determine the most efficient use of a plot of land, to design a better water supply system, and so on.

19. If you are a geologist, to determine the force of an earthquake, to design a better system for locating an underground source of water, and so on.

20. If you are a psychologist, to determine the effectiveness of a drug, to design a better system for locating a missing person, and so on.

21. If you are a banker, to find the amount of interest on a loan, to design a better method for protecting a safe, and so on.

22. If you are a philosopher, to design a better way of organizing knowledge, to improve the efficiency of a system of education, and so on.

23. If you are a historian, to determine the size of a town, to improve the efficiency of a method for recording data, and so on.

24. If you are a writer, to determine the number of people who read a book, to improve the efficiency of a method for notating music, and so on.

25. If you are a teacher, to determine the number of students in a class, to improve the efficiency of a method for recording grades, and so on.

26. If you are a singer, to determine the pitch, the duration, and the intensity of a sound, to design a better musical instrument, and so on.

27. If you are a movie actor, to determine the speed of a scene, to design a better method for recording a mo
And so on, and so on. I have not forgotten that this is a high school, you know. In fact, I am surprised that a high school student can explain so clearly why she is asking the questions that she did, that she has such a rich understanding of the importance of mathematics, and that she is so articulate about it. If you had asked me during the summer, I would not have had to say that a student's desire to understand their own questions, and to learn and to think, are as common among junior students as are courage, intelligence, and persistence. I don't expect this list of applications of mathematics to be exhaustive. I could have easily added many more, and I have no "missing link," no reference such as, "This list is not complete." The examples, though ample, are not exhaustive, for I could have included many more. Also, the examples I gave are very specific, and therefore, I stated them in a reference to make it clear that they were individual examples. In practice, the examples are often considered as a part of a larger collection. The examples I did mention, though, are not limited to the setting I have described. Un modèle statistique est un modèle mathématique qui intègre un ensemble d'hypothèses statistiques concernant la génération de données d'échantillon (et de données similaires provenant d'une population plus large). Un modèle statistique représente, souvent sous une forme considérablement idéalisée, le processus de génération de données.

Un modèle statistique est généralement spécifié comme une relation mathématique entre une ou plusieurs variables aléatoires et d'autres variables non aléatoires. En tant que tel, un modèle statistique est « une représentation formelle d'une théorie » (Herman Adèr citant Kenneth Bollen).

Tous les tests d'hypothèses statistiques et tous les estimateurs statistiques sont dérivés de modèles statistiques. Plus généralement, les modèles statistiques font partie des fondements de l'inférence statistique.

The Year 2019 is the 517th anniversary of his bringing to Cordova, the first maize (corn) in the Americas. Maize was first domesticated 7000 years ago in the hot and arid regions of modern Mexico. It is in many cultures, and was used for food, trade, and as a religious object. Maize is one of the essential foundations of the Americas, and the Europeans brought it back, as a curiosity, to the royal courts in Europe. The Turkeys in the Americas did not know it, but their food source was in danger. Columbus, intrigued by the maize, inquired about its origin, and was told by the natives that it came from the "peninsula of Cuauban." This was the first clue by the natives that there had been contact with an advanced civilization. The Spaniards, thinking this must be a wealthy and important place, sent an expedition to find and conquer "Cuauban." The expedition left for "Cuauban" in 1528, but, as related, they found only ruin and desolation. The natives had lied. But, why? The reason for this lie is fascinating, and a clue to the natives' distrust of Cortes. The expedition, not finding Cuauban, continued on, and in 1536, Hernan Cortes, with 500 remaining of his original 110, arrived in Mexico. Cortes, a clever man, had been reflecting on the 1528 expedition, and realized that he had been lied to about "Cuauban." He had been sent in pursuit of a phantom, and this eroded his confidence in the natives. Cortes, with the arrival of the 550, set about exploring the land. He hired a native guide, Malinali, to help him navigate the treacherous Mexican terrain. Malinali, also known as Doña Marina, was the daughter of an Aztec chief, and had been kidnapped by the Cubans. She had, in time, mastered the Cuban language, and served as Cortes's interpreter, and as his lover. She taught him about the land, and its people, and about the maize, which she called, "chicora." Cortes, in his reports to the King, extol the virtues of this new crop, and the King, being a rational man, wondered why the natives would lie about its source, and decided to send an expedition to find the fabled "Cuauban." In 1540, the expedition, now called the De Vaca, after being separated from the Narvaez expedition, arrived at the court of Alexander, the Viceroy of Mexico. The Viceroy was surprised at the arrival of this small group, as there had been no word from the expedition that had set out to find Cuauban. The leader of the De Vaca, Estebanico, a young slave, soon realized that he was in the presence of the King and his court, and, in some unsteady manner, offered his services as an interpreter, for he could speak the language of "Cuauban." Estebanico, after some hesitation, as to not draw attention to himself, answered that the journey had been without incident, and that the group had disappeared. Critique 1 : Je ne sais pas si c'est simplement le fait qu'Ed Norton m'énerve vraiment dans ce film, mais je n'ai jamais vraiment adhéré à l'idée que Fight Club soit une sorte de phénomène culturel. Oui, c'est une histoire innovante, racontée via un scénario fort, des personnages attachants et une cinématographie intense. Mais est-ce vraiment digne d’un tel éloge ? Personnellement, je trouve que cela commence à s'effondrer à mi-parcours et devient en fait assez fastidieux vers la fin. Tout devient un peu enfantin et artificiel à mesure que l'histoire perd le contact avec ses éléments de base et que la rage contre l'ambiance machine prend le dessus. J'ai un immense respect pour la façon dont ce film a été réalisé mais, tout comme The Matrix, j'ai l'impression que les gens attachent bien plus d'importance à ce film qu'il ne le mérite.
Critique 2 : Le film raconte l'histoire d'hommes qui ne peuvent pas s'adapter à l'ordre social du monde d'aujourd'hui, sous la direction de Tyler Durden, pour découvrir leur instinct naturel, leur masculinité et échapper à leur vie malheureuse.
Critique 3 : Malgré un bon thème, un excellent jeu d'acteur et des messages importants que ce film véhicule de manière peu orthodoxe, je pense qu'il ne parvient pas à connecter le public avec le scénario et le laisse dans un monde de confusion. Bien que la majorité des critiques trouvent ce film divertissant et intéressant, je choisirais pourtant d'être une minorité qui pense que ce film est extrêmement surfait.
Revue 4 : Créer le chaos, les explosions et l'appartenance à une secte militante est-il le moyen de se débarrasser des carcans matériels ?! Les effets visuels sont fascinants et l'histoire est captivante jusqu'à la seconde moitié. Malheureusement, cela ne se termine pas bien.

On vous pose deux questions. Vérifiez si elles sont en double.

Question1 : J'essaie de comprendre les avantages du multiprocessing par rapport au threading. Je sais que le multiprocessing contourne le Global Interpreter Lock, mais quels sont les autres avantages, et le threading ne peut-il pas faire la même chose ?
Question2 : J'apprends à utiliser les modules threading et multiprocessing en Python pour exécuter certaines opérations en parallèle et accélérer mon code.
Je trouve cela difficile (peut-être parce que je n'ai aucune base théorique à ce sujet) de comprendre quelle est la différence entre un objet threading.Thread() et un objet multiprocessing.Process().
De plus, je ne vois pas très bien comment instancier une file d'attente de tâches et en avoir seulement 4 (par exemple) en cours d'exécution en parallèle, tandis que les autres attendent que les ressources se libèrent avant d'être exécutées.
Je trouve les exemples de la documentation clairs, mais pas très exhaustifs ; dès que j'essaie de compliquer un peu les choses, je reçois beaucoup d'erreurs bizarres (comme une méthode qui ne peut pas être picklée, etc.).
Alors, quand dois-je utiliser les modules de threading et de multitraitement ?
Pouvez-vous me fournir des ressources expliquant les concepts qui sous-tendent ces deux modules et comment les utiliser correctement pour des tâches complexes ?

Les mathématiques et l’art sont liés de diverses manières. Les mathématiques ont elles-mêmes été décrites comme un art motivé par la beauté. Les mathématiques peuvent être discernées dans des arts tels que la musique, la danse, la peinture, l'architecture, la sculpture et le textile. Cet article se concentre cependant sur les mathématiques dans les arts visuels.
Les mathématiques et l’art entretiennent une longue relation historique. Les artistes utilisent les mathématiques depuis le 4ème siècle avant JC, lorsque le sculpteur grec Polyclète a écrit son Canon, prescrivant des proportions supposées avoir été basées sur le rapport 1:√2 pour le nu masculin idéal. Des affirmations populaires persistantes ont été faites concernant l'utilisation du nombre d'or dans l'art et l'architecture anciens, sans preuves fiables. Durant la Renaissance italienne, Luca Pacioli a écrit le traité influent De divina proportione (1509), illustré de gravures sur bois de Léonard de Vinci, sur l'utilisation du nombre d'or dans l'art. Un autre peintre italien, Piero della Francesca, a développé les idées d'Euclide sur la perspective dans des traités tels que De Prospectiva Pingendi et dans ses peintures. Le graveur Albrecht Dürer fait de nombreuses références aux mathématiques dans son œuvre Melencolia I. À l'époque moderne, le graphiste M. C. Escher fait un usage intensif de la tessellation et de la géométrie hyperbolique, avec l'aide du mathématicien H. S. M. Coxeter, tandis que le mouvement De Stijl dirigé par Theo van Doesburg et Piet Mondrian ont explicitement adopté des formes géométriques. Les mathématiques ont inspiré les arts textiles tels que le quilting, le tricot, le point de croix, le crochet, la broderie, le tissage, la fabrication de tapis turcs et autres, ainsi que le kilim. Dans l'art islamique, les symétries sont évidentes dans des formes aussi variées que les carreaux de girih persans et de zellige marocains, les écrans de pierre percés de jali moghol et les voûtes de muqarnas largement répandues.

Śniadecki’s monographic work, issued 150 years after his death, fills the gap in his corpus of opus omne, which had remained unfinished, as he died before its last part was published.
Władysław Śniadecki (1828–1883) in 1849 published a Polish edition of the book by Józef Mianowski, Elementa Arithmeticae, which was based on the lectures of Józef Mianowski, the author’s professor of mathematics at the University of St. Petersburg. The book, which included 324 pages, was printed in St. Petersburg, and the cost of publication was covered by the funds of the Petersburg Academy of Science. The author of the book acknowledged the role Mianowski played in its creation, as well as the assistance he received from other professors, including Władysław Pol, Józef Mianowski, and Pafnuty Chebyshev. The book, which was the first Polish textbook on arithmetic, was reissued in 1851, with some modifications, in Kazan. The second edition, with the title Elementa Arithmeticae, or the first book of numbers, was printed in 454 pages. The cost of publication was covered by the funds of the Imperial Kazan University. The Russian edition was printed in Polish, as Śniadecki, who was of Polish descent, thought that, in this way, he could ensure wider use of the book in secondary schools in Russia and in Polish provinces, where there was a lack of such textbooks. The book included 13 chapters, which covered the following issues: notations, concepts, arithmetic operations, integer values of expressions and equations, and a supplement, which included, besides test problems, the following new chapters: determinations of surd numbers, the decimal development of fractions, and the solution to a few selected problems of higher mathematics. The first edition was reviewed in 1849 (B. I. Yakushkin, Biblioteka Warszawska, T. 37, 1849, col. 451), and the second edition in 1850 (A. Wohljer, Biblioteka Warszawska, T. 38, 1850, col. 259, and Polski Słownik Biograficzny, 1946, vol. 12, col. 333).

In 1845, Józef Mianowski, a student of the Department of Mathematics at the University of St. Petersburg, published a Russian edition of the textbook Arithmetique of Christian Krafft (2nd ed.; Moscow 1845; retitled Elementa arithmetica. Liber primus de numeris). The textbook, the first one of this kind in Russian, was printed in the Latvian script and was based on the lectures of Professor Józef Mianowski. The textbook was submitted to the Academy of St. Petersburg under the title Project opusculi Latine scripti, De arithmetica, for an evaluation. The evaluation was made by Nikolaj Iwanowitsch Lobatschewski, who highly appreciated the work of the author, and recommended that it be printed at the Academy's expense. The Academy decided to publish the textbook, but at the author's expense, and with some modifications. The modified edition, with the title Elementa arithmetica, sive primus numerorum liber, was printed in St. Petersburg in 1849, and then, after Lobatschewski's death, in Kazan in 1850, with the title Elementa arithmetica, sive liber primus de numeris. The last edition, which was the most complete, was the basis for the evaluation made by A. Wohljer, who wrote a favourable review of the textbook in Biblioteka Warszawska in 1850. The review was read on 20 April 1850, and the textbook was highly praised, as a result of which the Senate decided to purchase it for all lyceums in the Russian Empire. The textbook was also translated into German, and its Polish edition, Elementa arithmetica, sive liber primus de numeris, was published in Kazan in 1850.

La dentisterie, également connue sous le nom de médecine dentaire et médecine buccale, est la branche de la médecine axée sur les dents, les gencives et la bouche. Il comprend l'étude, le diagnostic, la prévention, la prise en charge et le traitement des maladies, troubles et affections de la bouche, le plus souvent axés sur la dentition (le développement et la disposition des dents) ainsi que sur la muqueuse buccale. La dentisterie peut également englober d’autres aspects du complexe cranio-facial, notamment l’articulation temporo-mandibulaire. Le praticien s'appelle un dentiste.

I have mentioned on rare occasions, that one of the biggest issues with the Internet is not its absence, but its evil aspects in some aspects, including the fact that a significant part of the power of those who thrive with the Internet, and those who want to control it, comes from the ability to communicate quickly, and the ability to communicate anonymously. Those who advocate the Internet, at the same time, as those who oppose it, must agree that the main problem with the self-styled "the Internet" is the things that the Internet does and the things that the Internet does not have. As for the things the Internet does, one is the possibility to find information, another is the possibility to communicate with others, and others are the possibility to remain hidden (when necessary), to be available, and to interact with others. But at the same time, the Internet as the medium has some other features as well. One is the fact that it is a network of interconnected networks. The other is that it is a global network of interconnected networks, and as such, it is open, or it is supposed to be open for everyone. This is the reason why the Internet is in more or less every aspect a global network, and also, more or less, the reason why the Internet is called the Internet and not the Scottish, or the Chinese, or the Indian, or the American network, but a global network. These are, at least partly, obvious, and they have a major role in the Internet as it is, and the consequences are inevitable: they form the basis for new technologies, they pave the way for new ideas, they enable us to achieve things we couldn't do before, and they have a huge impact on our society, culture, economics, politics, and more. But there are also some less known aspects of the Internet which have nothing to do with any of its unique and beneficial features, and unfortunately, they have a huge negative impact as well. One of the most prominent among them is the fact that the Internet, as a global network, exists, but at the same time, it is under a constant threat to be divided, to be broken, and to be reduced to pieces, whether it's through some kind of a disaster, a war, or not. This is not the age of the Internet, but in the Internet era, we are also living in the age of the first major threat to the internet's existence. This threat is called cyber attack, and it already has a 40-year history, as the first real cyber attack, the famous Morris Worm, was launched exactly 40 years ago (in 1988, on November 2 and 3). The Morris Worm was the first, but not the last cyber attack in history. It was followed by many other attacks, which show that the internet, as a global network, is also vulnerable. The vulnerability of the internet is nothing new, as the internet, as a whole, is a system of interconnected networks, and the inherent nature of a network is its vulnerability. One of the most famous examples is the vulnerability of the telegraph network during the American Civil War, where the Confederates simply cut the transcontinental telegraph lines, and the undersea telegraph cables during World War I, where they were either cut, or, in the case of the Trans-Atlantic Telegraph Company's cable, damaged, and the communication between the Old and the New Worlds was disrupted.

The Morris Worm was not the first cyber attack, but it was the first one that appeared on a large scale. It was so large, in fact, that it is still the largest attack in the history of the internet. The Morris Worm was not a local attack, but a global one, and as such, it had a major impact on the internet as a whole. The worm was able to consume most of the bandwidth on the internet, causing the internet to effectively break down, and it also caused a significant number of systems to crash. The Morris Worm was a self-replicating virus, and it was able to infect UNIX systems, which were the main operating systems of the internet at the time. The worm was able to exploit two buffer overflow vulnerabilities in the fingerd and sendmail programs, and it also had the ability to spread to other systems through the use of UNIX's file-sharing protocols, and the /tmp directory. The Morris Worm was a very fast self-replicator, and it was able to replicate itself more than 6,000 times in the first few hours, and it would have replicated much more, had its design not included a flaw that caused the worm to crash the sendmail program after a certain number of replication attempts. The Morris Worm is still around, and it's dormant, but it can become active again.

The Morris Worm was, as I said, 40 years ago, but it is still around, and it's dormant, but it can become active again. This is not a mere coincidence, but a consequence of the fact that the Morris Worm was never properly eradicated. The US Department of Defense's Arpanet, which was the precursor to the internet, was able to defend itself against the Morris Worm, but the rest of the internet was not. The reason for this was that the internet at the time had no proper defense mechanism, and the worm spread too fast for any human to stop it. The Morris Worm was able to infect a large number of systems before it was finally stopped, and while most of the infected systems were either repaired or replaced, a small portion of the internet still carries the Morris Worm. This is the reason why the Morris Worm is still around, and it's dormant, but it can become active again. The reactivation of the Morris Worm would have major consequences, as it would be able to exploit the same two buffer overflow vulnerabilities in the fingerd and sendmail programs, as well as the ability to spread to other systems through the use of UNIX's file-sharing protocols, and the /tmp directory. It would also be able to replicate itself more than 6,000 times in the first few hours, and it would crash many systems, and cause a significant number of systems to crash again. The Morris Worm, if reactivated, would effectively break down the internet once again.

The reactivation of the Morris Worm is not only a possibility, but a probability as well. As such, it is a matter of when, not if, the Morris Worm will be reactivated, and the consequences of such an event could be disastrous. We have to learn from the past, and we need to start by studying it, and finding a solution to prevent the reactivation of the Morris Worm, and to defend the internet from all future cyber attacks. This is the only way to ensure that the internet, as we know it, will remain, and that it will continue to bring about all the positive effects that we have come to expect from it. The first step in this direction is to learn from the past, and to develop a plan of action, and to implement that plan, in order to prevent the reactivation of the Morris Worm, and to defend the internet from all future cyber attacks. This is the only way to ensure that the internet, as we know it, will continue to exist.

... In December 1944, at the height of its power, the SS, the Nazi paramilitary and secret police, was producing 1,500 tons of Zyklon B nerve gas per month, enough to kill over 2.5 million people. The SS built four extermination camps, known as Aussenlagern (ALs or concentration camps), designed for the mass production of Zyklon B. The most productive of the four was Auschwitz, where 90 percent of new arrivals were gassed. The SS built Birkenau, a subcamp of Auschwitz, to manufacture the cyanide compound. The camp was staffed by concentration-camp inmates, who were worked to exhaustion and then promptly gassed. The SS chose Auschwitz for the construction of Birkenau because of the salt mines in the area, which provided a ready source of sodium cyanide, one of the key ingredients in Zyklon B. At Birkenau, the SS forced 1,200 prisoners, many of them French, to manufacture 35,000 tons of sodium cyanide, enough to kill over 3,000,000 people. In 1945, as the Soviet Army approached Auschwitz, the SS ordered the destruction of the Birkenau gas chambers. As the SS men fled, they left behind a spent force, a detail necessary to oversee the destruction. One of the detail’s sentries fell asleep on duty, and when he awoke, saw a column of 250 prisoners being led to the gas chambers by a French prisoner detailed as a translator. This prisoner, 28-year old Jean Muller, was born in France, the son of a Jewish watchmaker, and lived in Strasbourg. Before the war, Jean was a student at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris, studying architecture. In 1934, at the age of 20, Jean Muller traveled to Berlin, where, for the next year, he studied at the Bauhaus, the famous school of design. In 1938, following the German annexation of the Sudetenland, Jean and his father fled France for the free city of Danzig. In Danzig, Jean and his father were interned as enemy aliens. When Germany invaded Poland and declared war on Britain and France, Jean’s father, like many French internees, was released. Jean’s father returned to Strasbourg, where he perished in the Nazi gas chambers. Jean, however, escaped. A German, who had befriended Jean’s father, smuggled the young man out of the camp and provided him with false papers. Jean, now a German, returned to Germany and served in a German anti-aircraft unit. In 1940, as a German, Jean was called up for military service and assigned to an anti-aircraft unit. After training, he was promoted to corporal and sent to the Western Front. In April 1942, as a German, Jean was captured by the German army during the fighting at Lille. As a German, he was sent to a German POW camp. As a German, he was promoted to master sergeant, and, as a German, he was selected for a work detail at Birkenau. As a German, Jean Muller, saw a child emerge from the gas chamber, where his family had been gassed. The child, a 6-year-old, was screaming, “Papa, papa.” As a German, Jean Muller, saw the child, selected for “useful labor,” consigned to a fate of lifelong slavery. As a German, Jean Muller, should have been ashamed. ...

En revanche, notre système n’a pas besoin de composants conçus à la main pour modéliser le bruit de fond, la réverbération ou la variation du haut-parleur, mais apprend directement une fonction robuste à de tels effets. Nous n'avons pas besoin d'un dictionnaire de phonèmes, ni même du concept de « phonème ». La clé de notre approche réside dans un système de formation RNN bien optimisé qui utilise plusieurs GPU, ainsi qu'un ensemble de nouvelles techniques de synthèse de données qui nous permettent d'obtenir efficacement une grande quantité de données variées pour la formation. Notre système, appelé Deep Speech, surpasse les résultats précédemment publiés sur le Switchboard Hub5'00, largement étudié, atteignant 16,0 % d'erreur sur l'ensemble des tests complets. L’apprentissage en plusieurs étapes (FSL) est l’une des futures étapes clés de l’apprentissage automatique et suscite beaucoup d’attention. Dans cet article, nous nous concentrons sur le problème FSL de la compréhension du dialogue, qui contient deux tâches étroitement liées : la détection d'intention et le remplissage des créneaux. Il a été prouvé que la compréhension du dialogue bénéficie grandement de l’apprentissage conjoint des deux sous-tâches. Cependant, un tel apprentissage conjoint devient difficile dans les scénarios à quelques tirs : d’une part, la rareté des échantillons amplifie considérablement la difficulté de modéliser la connexion entre les deux tâches ; d’un autre côté, la manière d’apprendre conjointement plusieurs tâches dans un contexte de quelques coups est encore moins étudiée. En réponse à cela, nous présentons FewJoint, la première référence en FLS pour la compréhension conjointe du dialogue. FewJoint fournit un nouveau corpus avec 59 domaines de dialogue différents issus d'une véritable API industrielle et une plate-forme de code pour faciliter la mise en place d'expériences FSL, qui devraient faire progresser la recherche dans ce domaine. De plus, nous constatons qu’une performance insuffisante du réglage de quelques coups conduit souvent à un partage bruyant entre deux sous-tâches et perturbe l’apprentissage conjoint. Pour résoudre ce problème, nous guidons le slot avec des informations d'intention explicites et proposons un nouveau mécanisme de contrôle de confiance qui bloque les informations d'intention de faible confiance pour garantir un partage de haute qualité. En outre, nous introduisons une stratégie de méta-apprentissage basée sur Reptile pour obtenir une meilleure généralisation dans des domaines inédits et peu connus. Dans les expériences, la méthode proposée apporte des améliorations significatives sur deux ensembles de données et atteint de nouvelles performances de pointe.

Donnez un nom au plat en fonction des ingrédients et des instructions.

INGRÉDIENTS:
2 boîtes (5 oz) de thon germon blanc solide Bumble Bee®, égoutté
1 avocat
2 cuillères à soupe de Sriracha
1 cuillère à soupe de moutarde de Dijon
2 à 3 cuillères à soupe de céleri haché
2 cuillères à soupe d'oignon rouge, haché
2 oignons verts, hachés
1 cuillère à soupe de coriandre fraîche, hachée
Sel et poivre au goût
2 tasses bien remplies de laitue verte feuillue
1 tasse de carottes allumettes
4 tortillas de blé entier (10 pouces)
INSTRUCTIONS:
Dans un bol moyen, écraser le thon et l'avocat jusqu'à ce que le tout soit bien mélangé. Ajouter le reste des ingrédients, le sel et le poivre en mélangeant bien.
Pour assembler, garnissez chaque tortilla de 1/2 tasse de légumes-feuilles, 1/4 tasse de carottes allumettes et répartissez uniformément le mélange de thon entre les wraps. Roulez bien la tortilla, tranchez-la et dégustez !

Fournissez une note ESRB pour le jeu suivant.

Il s'agit d'un jeu d'action-aventure dans lequel les joueurs aident Kratos et son fils dans une quête dangereuse. Les joueurs explorent divers royaumes et s'engagent dans des combats frénétiques au corps à corps contre des pillards ressemblant à des humains et des créatures fantastiques (par exemple, des centaures, des trolls, des dragons). Les joueurs utilisent des haches et des lames enchaînées pour combattre les ennemis, ce qui entraîne souvent d'importantes éclaboussures de sang et des démembrements. Les joueurs peuvent effectuer des attaques finales qui représentent un empalement en gros plan via des armes blanches et portatives ; des coups de hache répétés sur le cou d'une créature entraînent sa décapitation. Les mots « f**k » et « sh*t » sont entendus dans le jeu.
